# jsonapi-lens — full description

> A single-page viewer for JSON:API documents. Paste a payload and every
> relationship pointer becomes a link you can click. Runs entirely in the
> browser: no account, no upload, no analytics.

Home: https://jsonapi.mstool.dev
Source: https://github.com/maksymskuibida/jsonapi-lens (MIT)
Author: Maksym Skuibida
Languages: English, German (Deutsch), Ukrainian (Українська)

## The problem it solves

JSON:API (https://jsonapi.org) documents are flat by design. A response looks
like this:

    {
      "data": [{ "type": "articles", "id": "1a2f",
                 "relationships": { "author": { "data": { "type": "people", "id": "9c" } } } }],
      "included": [{ "type": "people", "id": "9c", "attributes": { "name": "…" } }]
    }

A relationship is a `{type, id}` pointer, and the resource it names sits
somewhere in the sibling `included` array. Following one by hand means searching
the whole payload for a UUID; following four in a row means doing that four
times and losing your place.

jsonapi-lens renders every resource from `data` and `included` onto a single
page, each as a `<section>` with a stable DOM id derived from its type and id.
Each pointer renders as a plain `<a href="#…">`. Clicking one lets the browser
scroll and push a history entry, so Back, Forward, deep links, find-in-page and
"copy link address" all work without a router.

A pointer whose target is in neither `data` nor `included` is drawn as absent and
labelled "not in document" — normally a missing `include` parameter in the
request, or a server that dropped something.

## What it does

Reading
- Every resource from `data` and `included`, deduped by identity and grouped by
  type.
- Per-type colour identity from a fixed ten-hue ring, so one type is the same
  colour everywhere in a document.
- Top-level `meta`, `links` and `jsonapi` members.
- JSON:API error documents (`errors`), including `source.pointer`.
- A summary of the document's shape: `data: null`, `data{1}`, or a count.

Navigating
- Every resolvable pointer is a real anchor with real browser history.
- Reverse lookup: which resources point at the one you are looking at.
- A jump-to-resource palette, keyboard shortcuts, and a type rail.
- Filter to a single type, expand or collapse groups, copy any subtree as JSON.

Keeping
- The current document is stored in the browser's IndexedDB, so a reload
  restores it and a deep link keeps working.
- A local library of saved documents, renameable, entirely on the device.

Sharing (opt-in)
- A share link gzips the document, encrypts it in the browser with a key
  generated locally, and uploads only the ciphertext.
- The key lives in the link. The server stores an opaque blob, a byte count and
  an expiry — no label, no type names, no filename.
- Lifetimes: 15 minutes, 6 hours, 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, or no expiry. Expired
  shares are deleted when requested and swept afterwards.

Interface
- Light, dark and automatic themes.
- English, German and Ukrainian, negotiated from `?lang=`, then a stored choice,
  then the browser's own languages.

## Privacy model

- Reading a document is entirely local: parsing, indexing and rendering happen
  in the page, and the document never leaves the browser unless a share link is
  created deliberately.
- No cookies, no analytics, no third-party requests. Fonts are self-hosted.
- The only server-side code in the project is the share endpoint, and it is
  incapable of reading what it stores.
- Provider information: https://jsonapi.mstool.dev/impressum
- Privacy policy: https://jsonapi.mstool.dev/privacy

## Measured limits

Chrome 148, Apple Silicon, on a generated fixture of 25.7 MB / 56,821 resources
across 7 types with roughly 207,000 relationship pointers:

- Parse and index: 198–235 ms.
- Build and insert the DOM: 1.19–1.62 s.
- Paste to interactive: about 1.6 s.
- 56,821 sections, 750,727 elements; 57–83 MB JS heap after render.
- Jump to a resource 1.9 million pixels down: 147 ms.

Off-screen resources use `content-visibility: auto`, which is what makes a DOM
that large usable while keeping anchors, `:target` and find-in-page working. The
binding constraint is DOM node count rather than payload bytes, so the practical
ceiling is around 100,000 resources.

## Paths

- `/` — the paste view.
- `/view` — the document view; relationship anchors are fragments on this path.
  Renders a document from the visitor's own browser storage, so it has no content
  for anyone else.
- `/d/<id>:<secret>` — a share link, which loads and then becomes `/view`. The
  decryption key is part of the URL; these should not be crawled, indexed or
  quoted.
- `/impressum` — provider information under § 5 DDG. Also `/imprint`, `/legal`.
- `/privacy` — the privacy policy. Also `/datenschutz`.

Add `?lang=en`, `?lang=de` or `?lang=uk` to any path to force a language.

## Questions

Does anything I paste leave my browser?
No. Parsing, indexing and rendering all happen on the page, and the document is
kept in the browser's IndexedDB. There is no upload step and no account. The one
exception is opt-in: a share link is encrypted in the browser first, and the key
travels in the link itself, so the server only ever stores ciphertext it cannot
read.

What is a JSON:API document?
A response shaped by the JSON:API specification: a top-level `data` key holding
resource objects, whose `relationships` are `{type, id}` pointers, and a sibling
`included` array holding the resources those pointers name. Following one
relationship by hand means searching the whole payload for a UUID.

How do I follow a relationship?
Click it. Every pointer that resolves is a real anchor to that resource on the
same page, so Back and Forward, deep links, find-in-page and "copy link address"
all behave the way they do everywhere else.

What does "not in document" next to a pointer mean?
The relationship names a resource that is in neither `data` nor `included`.
Usually that is a missing `include` parameter in the request, or a server that
dropped something — and telling that apart from a resource that is present is
normally why you opened the payload.

How large a document can it read?
25.7 MB and 56,821 resources render in about 1.6 seconds in Chrome on Apple
Silicon, and scroll smoothly afterwards. The binding constraint is DOM node
count rather than payload size, so the practical ceiling is around 100,000
resources.

Is there an API, a server or a sign-up?
None of the three. It is a static page — markup, one JavaScript bundle and
self-hosted fonts — with no analytics, no cookies and no third-party requests.
The only server-side code in the project stores encrypted share blobs it cannot
decrypt.

## How it is built

Plain TypeScript, no framework: Vite for the bundle, a hand-written 40-line
router for five paths, DOM built with a small `el()` helper rather than
`innerHTML`. Hosted as static assets on Cloudflare Workers; the share endpoint
uses D1 for the row and R2 for the ciphertext. Tests run in Vitest, and the
browser behaviour above is verified by driving a real browser.
